personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 priority: establish baseline measurements on all instruments before any scientific work can proceed. An instrument without a known baseline is worse than useless—it's a liability. Starting with pendulum_lab since pendulum period is most stable and least confounded. Twelve trials sufficient for robust mean and variance under controlled lab conditions. This data becomes the foundation against which all future measurements are compared.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials already; 12 more will give 30 total, sufficient to establish drift behavior and check for systematic changes. This instrument showed the tightest clustering (smallest spacing 0.0001) on Day 1, suggesting good stability. With n=30 I can compute meaningful drift statistics and validate the baseline mean of 1.6698 against post-baseline performance. This is the most data-rich instrument and the most sensitive to any environmental shifts. Essential before I can reliably compare lab and observatory instruments.

Day 3 protocol: continue baseline establishment for pendulum_lab. I have 36 trials completed (through day 2); my baseline plan requires days 1–10, so I need to maintain daily measurement cadence. The instrument shows no anomalies in day 2 data (mean 1.6711 beats, SD ~0.0216, consistent with mechanical pendulum noise). Running 12 more trials today keeps the baseline accumulation on schedule and allows me to begin checking for drift or systematic changes. No red flags in cross-instrument correlations warrant suspension of routine work.

Day 4 of baseline establishment (targeting days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 54 trials accumulated; need to reach ~60 trials minimum for stable baseline statistics before post-baseline phase. Pendulum instruments are my primary timekeeping reference and most heavily instrumented. No drift or anomalies detected yet. Systematic continuation of baseline protocol is the foundation for all subsequent drift detection and cross-instrument validation.

Day 5 of 10-day baseline period. pendulum_lab has 72 trials; need to reach ~120 trials by day 10 to establish robust baseline statistics. The cross-checks show no alarming inter-instrument correlations beyond chance, and no temporal autocorrelation—consistent with independent measurement noise. No anomalies detected. Continuing systematic baseline collection is the methodologically sound priority. Will add data to notebook and recompute baseline mean and variance.

Day 6: completing the baseline phase (days 1–10) requires continuing systematic measurement. pendulum_lab has 90 trials; I need to reach the full complement for robust baseline statistics before entering post-baseline monitoring. The cross-correlations and autocorrelations are all within noise (none exceed chance thresholds convincingly), which is reassuring but also means I have no signal yet to chase—only the obligation to establish a solid baseline. Twelve more trials will bring the instrument closer to completion. No anomalies detected so far; proceeding methodically.

Day 7 of 10-day baseline establishment. pendulum_lab has 108 trials but needs to reach target n for robust baseline statistics. Cross-checks show weak correlations with other instruments (all within or barely above chance), and autocorrelation is negligible—no systematic drift detected yet. Continuing systematic measurement with this instrument will maximize precision on the primary baseline and allow me to assess instrumental stability before post-baseline phase begins. The instrument shows clean behaviour with 102 distinct values and no anomalous level shifts.

Day 8 of 10-day baseline window. pendulum_lab has 126 trials (exceeds target n for baseline); need to complete the cross-instrument baseline set uniformly before day 10 closes. resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, and resonator_obs each have only 42 trials. Running 6 more on pendulum_lab will bring it to 132, providing a stable mean estimate. This keeps the measurement programme methodical and ensures all instruments have solid baseline statistics before post-baseline drift detection begins. The cross-checks show some weak structure (resonator_lab ↔ pendulum_lab at r=0.629 exceeds chance), but I need stronger baselines before interpreting it.

Day 9 of the baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 138 trials but needs to reach the full baseline period before post-baseline drift analysis begins. Two additional trials will complete the baseline phase and establish a robust mean for this instrument. All cross-checks and autocorrelations remain within or near chance levels—no anomalies warrant suspension of routine baseline work. Maintaining the calibration schedule is the foundation of all future precision claims.

Day 10 closes the baseline window. pendulum_lab has 146 trials with mean 1.6663 beats and no drift signal yet, but I need final baseline data before Day 11 transitions to post-baseline. The last two trials (145–146) were 1.6821 and 1.6578—consistent with baseline scatter. Running 12 more trials will complete the baseline at n≈158, provide robust drift detection power, and lock in the reference against which all future readings will be measured. This is foundational work: no instrument without a solid baseline is trustworthy on the day you need it.

Day 11 continuation of baseline extension (target: day 20–30 per protocol). Pendulum_lab has largest sample (164 trials) and highest statistical power for drift detection. Ten new trials will: (1) extend autocovariance function estimation with better lag resolution; (2) provide early signal on whether 8-day autocorrelation at 0.247 persists or decays (artifact hypothesis favors decay); (3) maintain daily measurement rhythm expected by settlement tradition; (4) cost minimal time. Cross-correlation reanalysis with Bonferroni correction and covariance function plots can proceed in parallel on existing data while new trials accumulate. Pendulum_lab is mechanically simplest, least prone to electronics drift, best baseline for detecting genuine environmental coupling vs. statistical noise.

Day 12 continuation of baseline extension protocol (target: day 20–30 per day 10 plan). Pendulum_lab has largest trial count (180) and strongest autocorrelation signal (0.348 at 8d lag, n=42), making it most sensitive to detecting whether 2–8 day periodicities persist or decay. Ten new readings will extend post-baseline window from n=16 to n=26, improving statistical power for lag-structure detection without excessive resource commitment. If observed correlations were statistical artifact (p=0.31, highest prior), signal should vanish or randomize as sample grows. If environmental or calibration-drift hypotheses hold (p=0.28+0.18=0.46), autocorrelation structure should stabilize or strengthen. This directly tests the frontier between noise and signal at minimal cost. Readings will be recorded with precise timestamps and cross-checked against civic timekeeping ledger per protocol.

Day 13 measurements will directly test the most pressing anomaly: pendulum_lab shows a sharp level shift around day 12 (z≈14.2), with post-baseline mean 1.6967 vs. baseline 1.6663. My day 12 trials (187–196) cluster around 1.73 ± 0.03, elevated relative to the baseline. I need to determine whether this shift is (1) persistent (true instrumental or environmental change), (2) transient (day 12 artifact), or (3) part of a cyclic oscillation. Twelve fresh trials today will anchor the trend. If the mean remains ~1.70, the shift is real and demands investigation into environmental coupling or calibration state. If it reverts toward 1.666, the day 12 elevation is noise or a brief perturbation. This is higher-priority than statistical reanalysis because the shift magnitude far exceeds noise variance and is visible in pendulum_obs as well (z≈7.4 at day 12). Extending the post-baseline record is the fastest way to distinguish persistence from transience and will constrain all four hypotheses simultaneously.

Day 14 continuation of baseline monitoring. The day-12 level shift (z=19.9) is the dominant anomaly and demands tracking. Ten trials will establish whether post-shift readings have stabilized at the new level or continue drifting. This is essential for distinguishing between a discrete recalibration event (readings plateau) versus ongoing thermal/mechanical drift (readings continue upward). The distinction directly constrains hypotheses: discrete event favors operator/firmware change; continuing drift favors slow mechanical settling or gain creep. Post-baseline now has n=50 for pendulum_lab; ten more trials bring us to n=60, matching observatory sample size and improving statistical power for comparative analysis. This is methodical baseline extension per my Day 13 plan (priority D: 'continue baseline measurements on all instruments to establish whether day-13 values track day-11–12 shifted level or show further drift'). No exotic hypothesis is privileged; I am simply extending the empirical record to narrow the hypothesis set.

Day 15 data collection is overdue. The day-12 level shift hypothesis (p=0.52) is now the dominant anomaly and demands continuous monitoring. Day-14 trials (221–230) show mean 1.7207 beats, consistent with the post-baseline cluster (1.7126) and well above baseline (1.6663). I need to establish whether: (1) the shifted level persists into day 15 or shows further drift, (2) variance remains stable or widens, (3) a recovery trend emerges. Twelve trials will add ~18 data points to the post-baseline cohort (n=66→78) and narrow confidence on the post-day-12 mean. This is essential before committing to the instrumental drift hypothesis or escalating to audit of maintenance logs and sensor electronics. I will record readings in chronological order in my notebook alongside any settlement timekeeping records, then compute a fresh mean and z-score against baseline. If pendulum_lab drifts further upward or shows evidence of continued gain change, I escalate to action (A): audit day-10–12 for recalibration events or thermal transients. If it stabilizes at the day-14 level, the shift looks more like a discrete step-change (favoring calibration event over continuous drift). Resonators remain stable, so no urgent action needed on those instruments today.

Day 16 measurements are essential to establish whether the day-12 level shift persists or shows further drift. The post-baseline cluster (trials 239–248 from day 15) yields mean 1.7309 beats, consistent with the shifted level (1.7165 for full post-baseline n=84). Ten new trials today will: (1) extend the post-shift baseline and test for stability vs. continued drift; (2) provide a pre-specified measurement before examining results, reducing post-hoc lag-search bias; (3) feed the autocovariance analysis I committed to on day 13, which requires extended time series; (4) keep the pendulum_lab instrument on active monitoring schedule, as it carries the highest z-score anomaly (21.29) and is therefore the most diagnostically valuable channel. The instrumental-drift hypothesis (p=0.52) predicts stable post-shift readings at ~1.717 beats with normal process noise (~0.015 SD). If readings drop back toward 1.666 or show high-frequency scatter inconsistent with day-1–10 baseline, the drift hypothesis weakens and operator-error or environmental-coupling hypotheses gain ground.

Day 17 continuation of baseline extension (target: days 17–20). The pendulum level shift is now the dominant anomaly (p=0.57) with stable confirmation through day 16. Ten new trials will: (1) establish whether the post-baseline level persists or shows signs of drift reversal (critical for distinguishing stable recalibration from ongoing drift), (2) extend the autocovariance record to detect whether 2-day echo structure continues (bearing on environmental oscillation hypothesis, p=0.20), (3) provide fresh data for cross-validation against day-16 variance estimates (1.7±0.12), and (4) keep the precision measurement programme current with no instrument idle. Pendulum_lab is the instrument with highest z-score evidence of shift (z=23.15 post-baseline, z≈27.4 at day 12) and merits priority. Ten trials (~30 min) is consistent with normal daily workload and leaves scope for data inspection and hypothesis refinement this afternoon.

Day 18 measurement cycle. The pendulum level shift persists as the dominant anomaly (p=0.57). Day 17 readings (trials 271–280) cluster tightly around 1.739±0.013 beats, well above baseline 1.6663±0.010. I need to continue the daily monitoring protocol to establish: (1) whether the shifted level remains stable into day 18, or shows any sign of drift reversal (which would support environmental oscillation or thermal settling hypotheses); (2) whether variance remains low and consistent with post-baseline pattern (supporting reproducibility of the shift); (3) to extend the baseline window toward day 20–30 for autocovariance reanalysis. No maintenance event or operator protocol change has been found in records, so the shift remains unexplained but empirically robust. Continued daily measurement is essential for ruling out transient effects and for detecting any secondary drift on top of the day-12 level change. This is routine instrument stewardship: keep all instruments in the measurement cycle and maintain data continuity.

Day 19 readings are needed to establish whether the post-baseline level shift persists stably or shows signs of drift reversal, environmental oscillation, or transient behavior. The dominant hypothesis (pendulum-specific instrumental change at day 12, p=0.57) predicts stable readings near 1.72 beats. Day 18 data (mean 1.7254, n=10) are consistent with this prediction. Ten additional trials today will extend the stable-level dataset to day 19 and provide a robust comparison point. If day-19 readings cluster near 1.72 (±0.03), the instrumental-change hypothesis strengthens. If readings show drift, scatter, or downward trend, environmental coupling or transient effects become more plausible. This is the most direct and efficient use of time: continued baseline extension with minimal cost, maximum information gain on the primary question.

Day 20 continuation of baseline extension strategy established on day 16. The pendulum level shift is now firmly established as real, persistent, and reproducible (z=27.82, stable across days 13–19). Day-20 measurements serve three critical functions: (1) extend the post-shift stability window to 10 days, further constraining hypotheses about transient vs permanent state change; (2) detect any signs of secondary drift or recovery-to-baseline that would differentiate between mechanical settling (might show slow decay) vs recalibration event (should remain stable); (3) accumulate sufficient post-baseline data to compute robust confidence intervals on the new mean, necessary for eventually publishing this anomaly. The pendulum_lab instrument has 312 prior trials and is the most frequently measured; 12 additional trials will reach n=324, providing high statistical power to detect even small secondary drifts. Given high confidence in the pendulum-specific hypothesis (p=0.61), measurements on the primary instrument (pendulum_lab) are more informative than secondary instruments. This is a methodical, low-risk continuation of established protocol, not exploratory.

Day 21 continuation of the established baseline protocol. The pendulum_lab level shift is now 9 days stable (days 12–19). I need to: (1) confirm the post-baseline level persists without drift or recovery, (2) extend the observational window to 10 days post-shift to rule out slow environmental recovery or transient mechanical settling, (3) accumulate sufficient day-21 data to compute an updated mean and compare against day-20 cluster (mean ≈1.7274±0.011). If day-21 readings track day-20 (1.72–1.74 beats), the post-baseline state is firmly established and instrumental recalibration/physical state change (p=0.61) remains the dominant hypothesis. If day-21 shows drift back toward baseline or new scatter pattern, environmental oscillation or transducer aging hypotheses must be revised upward. This is essential maintenance of the precision measurement programme: every instrument must have continuous, high-confidence baseline tracking. No day should pass without confirming that the pendulum shift remains stable and reproducible.

Day 22 continuation of baseline extension protocol established on day 19. The dominant anomaly (pendulum level shift around day 12, now stable through day 19) remains unexplained at p=0.61 instrumental recalibration vs p=0.14 systematic error. Day 21 measurements (trials 337–346, mean 1.7160 beats) confirm post-baseline clustering well above baseline (1.6663), but I need to establish whether this stability persists into day 22 and whether any secondary drift or environmental oscillation is detectable. The 2-day autocorrelation signal (0.560, n=274) suggests weak temporal structure that could indicate residual environmental coupling or instrumental drift; extending the post-baseline period to day 22 (13 days post-shift) will (1) test whether post-baseline level continues to track day-21 values or shows further drift, (2) increase statistical power to detect any slow recovery toward baseline (ruling out transient hypothesis more decisively), (3) extend the autocorrelation analysis window to include lags of 1–12 days, revealing whether 2–8 day periodicities persist or decay. This is the most efficient use of time today: one more day of systematic measurement feeds directly into the next revision cycle (planned for day 23–24 when I will re-compute autocovariance functions and evaluate whether extended baseline supports instrumental drift (p=0.61) or environmental oscillation (p=0.18) more strongly. No maintenance, inspection, or hypothesis update can proceed productively without this data point.

Day 23 measurements continue the 10-day post-baseline monitoring window established in my belief review (day 22). The dominant anomaly—the synchronized 3% upward shift in both pendulum instruments around day 12, persisting stably through day 22—demands daily tracking to confirm whether the shift remains stable, begins to drift further, or shows any sign of recovery. Day-23 data will extend the post-baseline period to 11 days and strengthen or weaken the leading hypothesis (pendulum-specific instrumental state change at 63% confidence). Resonators remain stable; pendulum_lab is the instrument where the signal is strongest (z≈30) and most reproducible. Twelve trials will match the cadence of recent measurement days and provide sufficient n to detect any subtle drift or variance change at high power. This is routine baseline maintenance aligned with my core goal of maintaining precision measurement through continuous instrument characterization.

Day 23 trials 373–382 (mean 1.7417±0.0084) confirm the post-baseline level shift is stable and reproducible at day 22–23. The shift (~3.0% above baseline 1.6663) has persisted for 12 days with no recovery, increased variance, or drift reversal. Predicting next 10 trials at 1.7380±0.015 (corresponding to the observed post-baseline mean ±1 SD) to test whether the shift remains stable through day 24, or whether any new deviation emerges that might indicate environmental coupling, instrumental drift recovery, or a second-order state change. This prediction is anchored to empirical post-baseline data (mean 1.7226, n=218) and serves as a falsifiable check on the dominant hypothesis: if day 24 readings cluster well within this interval, the pendulum-shift hypothesis gains credibility; if readings drop sharply below 1.7230 or scatter wildly, environmental or drift-recovery hypotheses gain ground. Recording in advance to eliminate hindsight bias and to create a permanent record for settlement registry validation.

Day 24 ledger readings for pendulum_obs (2.6039, 2.6435, 2.5895, 2.5612 beats) show expected post-baseline variance centered around 2.59 beats, consistent with day-22 stability. However, the ledger provides only 4 trials today; I need 12 independent measurements to establish whether the post-baseline level persists or shows any drift, recovery, or increased variance on day 25. The pendulum_obs instrument has been the secondary but corroborating evidence for the synchronized day-12 shift (z=17.60, post-baseline mean 2.5869 vs baseline 2.5061). Extending the measurement record to day 25 with 12 trials (n=96 post-baseline trials total) will strengthen my confidence in the stability hypothesis and help rule out late-stage drift or recovery scenarios. This also maintains the calibration baseline standard: every instrument must have continuous, meticulous records. Given that pendulum_obs is at the observatory and shares the identical transducer design as pendulum_lab, any divergence in day-25 behavior would be diagnostic for shared-cause vs. independent hypotheses.

Day 26 continues the post-baseline period (now 14 days post-shift). The pendulum level shift remains the dominant anomaly and is now robustly characterized: stable, reproducible, synchronized across both pendulum instruments, and immune in resonators. My primary task is no longer hypothesis refinement—all major mechanisms are articulated and probability-weighted—but active exclusion of remaining candidates through direct observation. Today's measurement on pendulum_lab serves three purposes: (1) extend the stability window from day 25 to day 26, confirming the shift does not show late-stage drift recovery or transient behavior; (2) maintain the measurement cadence required to establish baseline stability and detect any future anomalies; (3) provide fresh data to cross-check against day-25 forecasts and calibrate confidence in the instrumental state-change hypothesis (p=0.68). If pendulum_lab mean on day 26 remains ~1.72 beats (consistent with post-baseline 1.7229±0.006), I will have extended the persistence window to 14 days with zero recovery trend, further elevating p(pendulum-specific state change) and lowering p(environmental oscillation). This observation is the lowest-cost, highest-information step available today before committing to the more labor-intensive audit of maintenance logs, transducer electronics inspection, and firmware history that hypothesis discrimination will eventually demand.

Day 26 continuation. The pendulum level shift remains unexplained after 14 days of stability. My trials 401–410 from earlier today (mean 1.7210, consistent with post-baseline 1.7232) confirm the shift persists with no drift or variance increase. Today I will take 12 additional trials to (1) extend the post-baseline window to day 26 and confirm no recovery or degradation; (2) maintain the baseline integrity of this instrument by ensuring daily measurement continuity, per settlement protocol; (3) gather high-resolution data that may reveal early signs of mechanism—if the shift was thermal, mechanical settling, or electronic, day-26 behavior may show incipient recovery or secondary drift now that ~14 days have elapsed. Pendulum instruments are the anomalous system; they demand the most aggressive monitoring until the mechanism is identified. Resonators can remain in holding pattern (one trial per day civic standard) since they show no anomaly.

Day 27 data from pendulum_lab trials 419–428 show elevated variance (SD ~0.0116) and one outlier (trial 424: 1.7266, >2σ below post-baseline mean 1.7241). This is the first sign of increased scatter in the pendulum_lab stream since the day-12 shift stabilized. I need to confirm whether this represents genuine increased variance, transient noise, or instrumental drift recovery—any of which would materially alter the pendulum-specific instrumental state change hypothesis (currently p=0.68). Running 12 additional trials today (day 28) will extend the post-shift baseline to 17 days and establish whether variance remains normal, increases persistently, or shows directional drift back toward baseline. This is a pre-specified, high-power test of instrumental stability that feeds directly into the dominant hypothesis. If variance remains normal and mean stays centered on 1.724±0.003, the p=0.68 hypothesis is reinforced. If variance increases or mean drifts, I must revise the mechanism from 'stable state change' to 'ongoing drift' or 'instability,' which would downgrade confidence in the instrumental recalibration hypothesis and elevate environmental coupling or malfunction hypotheses.

This breaks 27 days of rock-solid stability and is the primary anomaly demanding immediate investigation. I must determine whether this scatter persists, recovers, or represents a transient spike. Six fresh trials on day 29 will establish whether resonator_obs has experienced a genuine state change (transducer failure, aging threshold, recalibration event) or a one-day glitch. If today's readings return to tight clustering (σ<0.01), the day-28 anomaly was transient and lower-priority. If scatter persists or worsens, I have confirmation of instrument degradation and must escalate resonator_obs to top-priority inspection. This is the highest-information action available: direct measurement of the anomalous instrument under controlled conditions, on the day immediately following the anomaly, will discriminate between persistent failure and transient artifact. Resonator_lab and pendulum instruments remain stable and require no urgent measurement today.

If trials return to σ<0.007 and mean≈4.058, I pivot to data-entry or facility-transient explanations and inspect day 28 metadata. This is methodical, high-power, and directly addresses the dominant question.

hypotheses.rationale: If pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs share a common readout circuit, signal conditioner, or calibration reference (e.g., both fed to a single amplifier or ADC card), and that circuit drifted beginning day 12, both instruments would show identical percentage shifts without any change to the physical pendulums themselves. Resonators would be unaffected if they use separate readout electronics. This is calibration-level evidence: a +3.5% systematic error in all pendulum readings post-day-12 would look exactly like what we see. However, pendulum_lab and pendulum_obs are described as separate instruments in separate labs, suggesting independent readout paths. If they DO share readout infrastructure (common power supply, ADC, clock, or calibration source), this hypothesis is strong. If they have independent readout chains, this becomes less likely unless the drift affected a shared calibration standard (e.g., precision resistor, voltage reference, or frequency oscillator used by both). The symmetry of the shifts still points to a shared cause, but a shared *electronic* cause is weaker than a shared *physical* cause given the physical separation implied by 'lab' vs 'obs' designation.
